<body>

<header class="hero">
  <div class="wrap">
    <h1>Who controls the Algorithm?</h1>
    <p class="sub">Governing military AI, autonomous weapons, and cyber conflict</p>
    <div class="byline"><span>By <b>Mahad Shah</b></span><span>Research paper</span></div>
    <figure>
      <img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Collage of a soldier with a tablet, a drone, a bombed city, the UN chamber and scales of justice">
      <figcaption>Image created using ChatGPT</figcaption>
    </figure>
  </div>
</header>

<main class="wrap">

<section class="summary" aria-label="Key points">
  <ul>
    <li>The real question is who regulates military AI, not whether it is used.<span>Overview</span></li>
    <li>Humans must keep authority over decisions that end in death.<span>Autonomous weapons</span></li>
    <li>Regulation should be international, with states still held accountable.<span>Governance</span></li>
  </ul>
</section>

<section class="part" id="overview">
  <header><h2>Overview</h2></header>
  <div class="body">
    <p>There are many applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern armed conflicts. AI can assist with image interpretation, intelligence processing, logistical organisation, threat analysis, cyber security, and military strategic decisions. While certain applications might help lower soldier risks and increase analytical efficiency, others pose great concerns relating to the safety of civilians, accountability, cyber threats, and international stability.</p>
    <p class="pull">The question is less whether nations should deploy military AI, and more who has jurisdiction over its regulation, and under what limitations.</p>
    <p>This topic is particularly significant to autonomous weapons and AI-enabled cyber warfare. Autonomous weapon systems might recognise, track, and destroy specific objects independently once activated, with minimal further human intervention. AI can also facilitate attacks on military networks and civilian infrastructures, such as hospitals, electrical plants, transportation hubs, communication channels, and emergency services. International humanitarian law applies to all kinds of weapons systems, regardless of technology employed (ICRC, 2026). States, international lawyers, and humanitarian organisations debate whether current legislation suffices or whether new, legally binding regulations are needed.</p>
    <p>I would argue that the deployment of military AI should be governed through international cooperation. Although states retain overall jurisdiction and liability over AI-powered weapons in conflicts, they should refrain from unilaterally creating international laws regulating AI. Negotiation should occur within the UN structure and involve stakeholders from across continents: governments, militaries, AI developers, corporations, legal experts, humanitarian agencies, civil-society representatives, and global South states. The primary goals are <mark>preserving human autonomy in warfare decision-making</mark>, avoiding illegal harm to civilians, and minimising cyber conflict.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="part" id="autonomous-weapons">
  <header><h2>Autonomous weapons and meaningful human control</h2></header>
  <div class="body">
    <p>The type of AI weaponry generating the most controversy is autonomous weapons. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) defines autonomous weapon systems (AWS) as capable of identifying objects, choosing targets, and applying lethal or harmful force without further human intervention after initial activation (ICRC, 2026). Identifying a target can include searching for, recognising, selecting, and tracking targets that meet predefined criteria. Applying force involves destruction or disabling.</p>
    <p>AWS must be distinguished from general military AI. AI can translate languages, estimate mechanical breakdown probabilities, interpret satellite imagery, optimise logistics chains, and detect cybersecurity threats. These uses have their own ethical, methodological, or privacy problems, but they are fundamentally distinct from weapons because they never involve a decision-making procedure for lethal attacks.</p>

    <figure class="slot">
      <div class="art">
        <svg viewBox="0 0 640 230" role="img" aria-label="Three legal tests: distinction, proportionality, precautions">
          <g>
            <rect class="box" x="8" y="10" width="198" height="210" rx="8"/><rect class="brand" x="8" y="10" width="198" height="8" rx="4"/>
            <text x="24" y="58" font-size="22" font-weight="800">Distinction</text>
            <text x="24" y="92" class="sm">Is this a combatant</text><text x="24" y="112" class="sm">or a civilian?</text>
            <circle cx="70" cy="170" r="14" class="brand"/><circle cx="140" cy="170" r="14" fill="none" stroke="var(--signal)" stroke-width="4"/>
          </g>
          <g>
            <rect class="box" x="221" y="10" width="198" height="210" rx="8"/><rect class="brand" x="221" y="10" width="198" height="8" rx="4"/>
            <text x="237" y="58" font-size="22" font-weight="800">Proportionality</text>
            <text x="237" y="92" class="sm">Is the expected harm</text><text x="237" y="112" class="sm">worth the gain?</text>
            <path class="ln" d="M270 190h100M320 190v-40M280 150h80"/><rect x="266" y="150" width="28" height="12" class="signal"/><rect x="346" y="140" width="14" height="10" class="brand"/>
          </g>
          <g>
            <rect class="box" x="434" y="10" width="198" height="210" rx="8"/><rect class="brand" x="434" y="10" width="198" height="8" rx="4"/>
            <text x="450" y="58" font-size="22" font-weight="800">Precautions</text>
            <text x="450" y="92" class="sm">Was every step taken</text><text x="450" y="112" class="sm">to limit the harm?</text>
            <path d="M533 140l30 12v22c0 16-14 26-30 32-16-6-30-16-30-32v-22z" class="brand"/><path d="M520 176l9 9 17-20" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="5" fill="none"/>
          </g>
        </svg>
      </div>
      <figcaption>The three principles of international humanitarian law that autonomous weapons struggle to meet.</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <p>The core dilemma is differentiating lawful targets from civilians. International humanitarian law requires warring sides to distinguish combatants from civilians, strike only legitimate military objects, refrain from unnecessary civilian casualties, and prepare before launching attacks. These are the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions. Complying requires context-based assessment, not just identifying weapons or vehicles. As Winter (2020) demonstrated, autonomous weapons may have object and pattern recognition yet lack the contextual understanding to tell civilians and combatants apart in complex wartime situations. This matters most in urban warfare, where civilians live alongside armies and other protected objects.</p>
    <p>Proportionality presents another obstacle. Even if an object is a proper target, an attack may become impermissible when the expected civilian cost is excessive compared with the benefit. Such evaluations require human judgement, which autonomous weapons lack, especially since warfare entails considerable uncertainty (Winter, 2022). Humans must estimate probabilities and potential effects.</p>
    <p>For this reason, researchers and humanitarian agencies advocate <mark>"meaningful human control"</mark> over weapons and operational decisions. Santoni de Sio and van den Hoven (2018) argue that a system must be "traceable" by those who understand its functionality, and "trackable" by those who evaluate the moral justification for decisions. People deploying AI must understand the weapon's operational capacity, range, dangers, and deactivation protocols. The notion is therefore more than pressing a button to start an autonomous process.</p>

    <figure class="slot">
      <div class="art">
        <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-label="Decision loop where a human judges between the AI recommendation and the action">
                    <path class="ln" d="M150 100h50M200 100l-8-6M200 100l-8 6M330 100h40M370 100l-8-6M370 100l-8 6M510 100h40M550 100l-8-6M550 100l-8 6"/>
          <rect class="box" x="10" y="60" width="140" height="80" rx="8"/><text x="80" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" font-size="18">AI senses</text><text x="80" y="118" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">detects and tracks</text>
          <rect class="box" x="200" y="60" width="130" height="80" rx="8"/><text x="265" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" font-size="18">AI suggests</text><text x="265" y="118" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">ranks options</text>
          <rect class="signal" x="370" y="40" width="140" height="120" rx="8"/><text x="440" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" font-size="20" class="on-fill">Human judges</text><text x="440" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" class="on-fill">questions, rejects,</text><text x="440" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" class="on-fill">or halts</text>
          <rect class="box" x="550" y="60" width="80" height="80" rx="8"/><text x="590" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" font-size="18">Act</text>
        </svg>
      </div>
      <figcaption>Meaningful human control puts judgement between the algorithm's suggestion and the use of force.</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <p>Ekelhof describes at least three important functions of meaningful human control. Humans act as safeguards against illegal use and malfunctions. Human control guarantees legal accountability if a weapon commits an illegal act. And it ensures human autonomy in morally responsible decisions about deadly force. In other words, humans can question algorithms, reject their suggestions, and halt operations (Amoroso &amp; Tamburrini, 2021).</p>
    <p>Accountability is the central argument for international regulation. When an illegal act harms civilians during warfare, autonomous weapons and algorithms cannot be held criminally liable. Responsibility should fall on state authorities, military officials, weapon purchasers, manufacturers, programmers, or the corporation itself. Accountability involves answering for illegal or wrongful actions in court (Galliot, 2023). Internationally wrongful acts performed with the help of AI systems remain the responsibility of the party using the technology (Sassoli et al., 2023). Governments cannot bypass international accountability for unlawful acts committed by autonomous weapons.</p>
    <p>Hence the ICRC proposes banning AWS whose consequences cannot be foreseen and regulated adequately, alongside AWS designed to attack civilians directly. Other autonomous technologies should face strict regulation depending on their intended targets, operation period, scale of impact, and degree of human involvement (ICRC, 2026). The proposal limits AWS deployment without eliminating all military applications of AI.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="part" id="cyber">
  <header><h2>AI and cyber operations: the risk of escalation</h2></header>
  <div class="body">
    <p>Modern cyber operations include intelligence gathering, obtaining tactical advantages, sabotage, spreading misinformation, and attacking essential infrastructure. With AI, military units can interpret massive amounts of data simultaneously, conduct reconnaissance automatically, create fake phishing messages, and spread disinformation campaigns. These activities endanger critical civilian infrastructure because modern economies depend heavily on complex computer systems. International humanitarian law applies to cyberattacks against power grids, drinking water facilities, hospitals, telecommunication networks, transport services, and financial institutions (Haataja, 2022). A cyberattack on a nation's critical infrastructure can cause multiple disasters at the same time.</p>
    <p>Autonomous weapons may also appear within cyber operations. Biontino warns that AI cyber weapons may spread unintentionally, enter extraterritorial zones, damage civilian networks, and persist after military shifts.</p>

    <figure class="slot">
      <div class="art">
        <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-label="Attribution chain: attacker, proxy, spoofed signature, wrong target retaliated against">
          <path class="ln" stroke-dasharray="6 6" d="M110 85h60M270 85h60M430 85h60"/>
          <circle cx="70" cy="85" r="40" class="brand"/><text x="70" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" class="on-fill" font-size="15">Attacker</text>
          <circle cx="220" cy="85" r="40" class="box"/><text x="220" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" font-size="15">Proxy</text>
          <circle cx="380" cy="85" r="40" class="box"/><text x="380" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" font-size="14">Spoofed</text><text x="380" y="99" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" font-size="14">signature</text>
          <circle cx="570" cy="85" r="50" class="signal"/><text x="570" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" class="on-fill" font-size="14">Wrong state</text><text x="570" y="99" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="800" class="on-fill" font-size="14">retaliated on</text>
        </svg>
      </div>
      <figcaption>Attribution is hard: AI can forge signatures that point retaliation at the wrong adversary.</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <p>Attribution is a key concern. Determining who initiated an attack is difficult because attackers conceal identities, use proxies, manipulate digital footprints, and use spoofed code. AI might worsen this by helping adversaries forge false digital signatures or copy the stylistic features of another country's cyber unit, which may provoke retaliation against the wrong adversary.</p>
    <p>AI also risks accidental escalation through accelerated decision-making. Fast evaluation is useful, but a commander relying on algorithmic outputs may order retaliatory strikes based on incomplete or flawed intelligence. To prevent automation bias and AI-related misjudgments, <mark>human verification and monitoring of all AI-generated estimations remain essential</mark> before drastic decisions in warfare or cyber operations.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="part" id="governance">
  <header><h2>The governance of military AI: who should make the rules?</h2></header>
  <div class="body">
    <p>Governing military AI requires international cooperation among all nations because AI affects international peace, security, civilian safety, national sovereignty, and balances of power. Nonetheless, states retain overall jurisdiction because they command armed forces, engage in warfare, and bear international legal liabilities. International law, including the UN Charter, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and international criminal law, applies to all autonomous weapon systems (United Nations General Assembly, 2024). Within the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), the Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) drafted a provisional document on lethal autonomous weapon systems (LAWS), considering requirements for human judgement and control to guarantee compliance with distinction, proportionality, and precaution (CCW GGE LAWS, 2025).</p>

    <figure class="slot">
      <div class="art" style="padding:1.5rem">
        <ul class="chips">
          <li class="hl">UN framework</li><li class="hl">States</li><li>Militaries</li><li>AI developers</li><li>Corporations</li><li>Legal experts</li><li>Humanitarian agencies</li><li>Civil society</li><li>Global South states</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <figcaption>Who should be in the negotiation. Replace this block with a photo or graphic of your own.</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <p>State representatives should consult technical AI experts, lawyers, humanitarian organisations, and civil-society organisations. Participation from developing countries is highly important so that powerful states and private firms do not regulate these technologies unilaterally. Consensus on regulating LAWS is difficult because of disagreements over definitions of autonomy, concerns about military superiority, verification challenges, and fears of impeding innovation. Nevertheless, in 2025, 42 countries endorsed further negotiation on lethal autonomous weapon systems via the CCW platform (Reaching Critical Will, 2025).</p>
    <p>International approaches should therefore combine prohibition, regulation, and accountability, including mandatory evaluations, operating restrictions, human monitoring, emergency shutdown possibilities, and tracking of decisions.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="part" id="conclusion">
  <header><h2>Conclusion</h2></header>
  <div class="body">
    <p>While AI assists armed forces with intelligence analysis, logistical coordination, cybersecurity management, and military planning, it creates grave risks once machines can select targets, recommend the use of violence, and attack civilian infrastructure. Autonomous weapons may impair human control and protection during warfare, while AI-powered attacks on civilian infrastructure threaten to escalate into full-scale conflicts.</p>
    <p class="pull">The issue is less about outlawing all military AI, and more about ensuring humans retain authority over decisions that result in fatalities.</p>
  </div>
</section>
